title: 4Sum II
prompt: Given four integer arrays `nums1`, `nums2`, `nums3`, and `nums4`, all of length `n`, return the number of tuples `(i, j, k, l)` such that `nums1[i] + nums2[j] + nums3[k] + nums4[l] == 0`. Indices for each array are chosen independently (i, j, k, l each range over their own array, with no requirement that they be distinct from each other across arrays).

examples.explanation: With only one element per array, the only possible sum is 1+1+1+1=4, which never equals 0, so no valid tuples exist.

hints: Checking all combinations directly is O(n^4). Splitting the four arrays into two halves opens up a meet-in-the-middle approach.
Precompute every possible sum of one element from nums1 with one from nums2, and count how often each sum value occurs.
For every pair from nums3 and nums4, look up how many nums1+nums2 pairs equal the negation of that sum — a hash map turns this lookup into O(1) per pair, giving O(n^2) total instead of O(n^4).

solution.approach: Split the four arrays into two halves. Compute every possible sum of a pair (a from nums1, b from nums2) and store the frequency of each sum value in a hash map — this takes O(n^2) time over n^2 pairs. Then iterate every pair (c from nums3, d from nums4) and look up how many nums1+nums2 pairs summed to exactly -(c+d) in that map, adding the count to the running total. This meet-in-the-middle technique turns the naive O(n^4) quadruple-nested search into O(n^2) time (and O(n^2) space for the map).
